summary: Hybrid key exchange combines several key exchange algorithms so a connection stays secure as long as at least one of them holds. It is motivated by the move to post-quantum cryptography. This Informational document provides a construction for hybrid key exchange in TLS 1.3.

plainLanguage.summary: Lock a box with two different locks. A thief has to pick both, so it stays safe if one lock turns out to be weak.

questions: how to combine key exchange algorithms
subtitle: Glue two key exchanges together in TLS 1.3 by concatenating their keys and secrets, so the session holds if either one holds.

tldr.problem: Post-quantum key exchange algorithms are newer and less studied than the traditional ones, yet harvest-now-decrypt-later attackers may record handshakes today and break them later.
tldr.mechanism: Each hybrid combination gets its own NamedGroup. The key shares from the component algorithms are concatenated into one key_exchange value, and the component shared secrets are concatenated and fed into the TLS 1.3 key schedule where the (EC)DHE secret normally goes.
tldr.outcome: The session key stays secure as long as at least one component is unbroken. The RFC is Informational and works only for algorithms whose keys, ciphertexts and secrets have a fixed length.

today: RFC 9954 is an Informational document, published July 2026, and the metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on TLS 1.3 as specified in RFC 9846 and uses the terminology of RFC 9794.

sections.title: Goals and Scope
sections.content:
This document gives a simple concatenation-based construction for hybrid key exchange in TLS 1.3. Each hybrid combination is treated as one new key exchange method, negotiated and transmitted with existing TLS 1.3 mechanisms. A hybrid uses two or more algorithms based on different cryptographic assumptions, so the final session key is secure while at least one component stays unbroken.

It covers hybrid ephemeral key exchange only. It does not pick which next-generation algorithms to use, nor define their identifiers or encodings, and it does not address authentication with them, since session authentication cannot be broken retroactively.

The stated goals include backwards compatibility with endpoints that are not hybrid-aware, high performance, low latency, no extra round trips and minimal duplicate information. The motivation includes retroactive decryption (harvest-now-decrypt-later) and the lower confidence in newer algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan is to use a new lock and an old lock together, without making the door take longer to open or breaking doors that only have one lock.

sections.title: Key Exchange as a KEM
sections.content:
The RFC models key agreement as a key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) with three algorithms: KeyGen() returns a public key and secret key, Encaps(pk) returns a ciphertext and shared secret, and Decaps(sk, ct) returns the shared secret. Diffie-Hellman can be seen as a KEM too.

Because TLS 1.3 does not require ephemeral public keys to be used only once, any KEM used this way MUST be designed to be secure if the public key is reused. For generic KEMs that means IND-CCA2 security or a transform such as the Fujisaki-Okamoto transform. Implementations that reuse keys MUST stay within the KEM's bounds on reuse, and MUST NOT reuse randomness when generating KEM ciphertexts.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender seals a secret in a box using the receiver's open padlock. Only the receiver's key opens it. The padlock must stay safe even if it gets used more than once.

sections.title: Negotiating a Hybrid Group
sections.content:
Each combination of algorithms is represented by a NamedGroup and sent in the supported_groups extension. The identifier is opaque, with no internal structure implied, and it corresponds to an ordered pair of two or more algorithms. Pure post-quantum methods would need their own identifiers.

For IANA, hybrid identifiers come from a range distinct from the Finite Field Groups range, the Recommended column SHOULD be N, and the DTLS-OK column SHOULD be Y.
sections.plainLanguage: Each pair of locks gets a single name, like a menu item, and the client and server pick from the menu.

sections.title: Sending Keys and Ciphertexts
sections.content:
The public keys or ciphertexts of the components are concatenated into the key_exchange field of one KeyShareEntry, with no extra encoding or length fields. The order MUST match the order in the NamedGroup definition. The client's value holds the concatenated pk outputs, or the (EC)DH ephemeral share. The server's value holds the concatenated ct outputs, or its (EC)DH share.

TLS 1.3 requires key_exchange values in each entry to be generated independently. This RFC relaxes that so one ClientHello may reuse the same component value across entries, while values for different algorithms MUST still be independent.

The field is limited to 2^16-1 bytes. All defined ML-KEM parameter sets fit, though the ClientHello may then exceed one packet. Offering two hybrids with the same ML-KEM-768 part sends that key twice.
sections.plainLanguage: You tape the two keys together and send them as one package, always in the same order, so the other side knows where one ends and the next begins.

sections.title: Combining the Shared Secrets
sections.content:
The shared secrets are concatenated, again with no length fields: concatenated_shared_secret = MyECDH.shared_secret || MyPQKEM.shared_secret. This value goes into the TLS 1.3 key schedule in place of the (EC)DHE shared secret, as the input to the HKDF-Extract that produces the Handshake Secret.

For FIPS purposes, the RFC notes that NIST SP 800-56C lists simple concatenation as an approved way to generate a hybrid shared secret when one constituent comes from an approved method.
sections.plainLanguage: Both secrets are written one after the other on a single strip of paper, and that strip is what the rest of the handshake uses.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The result should be secure as long as one component is unbroken. With fixed-length secrets, the construction matches the dual-PRF combiner of Bindel et al., which preserves security if the hash function is a dual-PRF.

KEMs MUST resist public key reuse. ML-KEM does, but some IND-CPA-only lattice KEMs are vulnerable to private key recovery after a few thousand samples. Lengths must be constant, because variable-length secrets can create timing side channels (the Lucky Thirteen and Raccoon attacks are cited) and risks if the KDF hash loses collision resistance. This specification MUST only be used with algorithms that have fixed-length shared secrets once the NamedGroup is fixed.
sections.plainLanguage: Pieces must always be the same size, or an attacker could learn things from how long the work takes or mix up where one piece stops.

items.title: Backwards compatibility
items.text: Hybrid-aware parties stay compatible with ones that are not.

items.title: High performance
items.text: Hybrid use should not be prohibitively expensive.

items.title: Low latency
items.text: No substantial increase in connection setup time.

items.title: No extra round trips
items.text: In any of the three aware or unaware combinations.

items.title: Minimal duplicate information
items.text: Avoid sending multiple public keys of the same type.
